data.text: Terrence LeVarr Thornton (born May 13, 1977), better known by his stage name Pusha T, is an American rapper.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: He rose to prominence as one half of the Virginia-based hip hop duo Clipse, which he formed with his older brother Malice.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: Established in 1994, the duo were discovered by Pharrell Williams and signed with his record label Star Trak Entertainment, an imprint of Arista Records, in 2001.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: They initially released three studio albums—Lord Willin' (2002), Hell Hath No Fury (2006) and Til the Casket Drops (2009)—to mild commercial success; the former spawned the Billboard Hot 100-top 40 singles "Grindin'" and "When the Last Time", for which they became best known.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: After the duo disbanded in 2010, Thornton began pursuing a solo career.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: He signed with Kanye West's record label GOOD Music, an imprint of Def Jam Recordings following his work on West's fifth album, My Beautiful Dark Twisted Fantasy (2010); he featured on the singles "Runaway"—which peaked at number 12 on the Billboard Hot 100—and "So Appalled".
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: He released his first two solo projects—Fear of God and Fear of God II: Let Us Pray—in 2011, before releasing his debut studio album, My Name Is My Name (2013).
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: A critical and commercial success, it peaked at number four on the Billboard 200 and was followed by his second and third albums King Push – Darkest Before Dawn: The Prelude (2015) and Daytona (2018), which peaked at numbers 20 and three on the chart, respectively.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: His fourth album, It's Almost Dry (2022), became his first to debut atop the Billboard 200.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: Clipse briefly reunited to self-release their fourth album, Let God Sort Em Out (2025), which peaked at number 4 on the Billboard 200.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: West appointed Thornton as president of GOOD Music in 2015, where he remained one of the label's flagship artists until his departure in 2022.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: Three years later, he parted ways with his remaining label, Def Jam Recordings, due to creative disagreements.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: In 2020, he launched his record label Heir Wave Music Group, which aims as a platform for Virginia-based artists.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: Thornton has won a Grammy Award from six nominations.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: Pusha T was born Terrence LeVarr Thornton on May 13, 1977, in the Bronx borough of New York City to Gene and Mildred Thornton, though the family soon relocated to Virginia Beach, Virginia, where he and his brother, Gene Thornton Jr., grew up.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: As teenagers, the brothers both sold drugs, with Gene eventually being kicked out of their parents' house after they discovered what he was doing.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: In 1992, alongside his brother, Thornton began to pursue a career in hip hop, forming a group known as Clipse.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: His older brother Gene was known for most of the group's duration as Malice (the two were originally known as Terrar and Malicious, respectively).
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: Shortly after forming Clipse, the brothers were introduced to record producer and fellow Virginian Pharrell Williams of The Neptunes, who helped them secure a recording contract with Elektra Records in 1997.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: Terrence initially took the stage name Terrar.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: After being signed to Elektra, they began working on their debut album, Exclusive Audio Footage.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: After recording the entire album, they released one single, "The Funeral", which was commercially unsuccessful and eventually led to the release of the album being cancelled and Clipse being dropped from the label shortly after.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: After being dropped, Terrar changed his name to Pusha T, and despite not being signed to a major label, he made numerous appearances on other artists' songs, appearing on Kelis' 1999 single "Good Stuff" and Nivea's 2001 single "Run Away (I Wanna Be with U)", respectively, thanks to his relationship with The Neptunes, who produced both songs.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: In early 2001, Pharrell Williams signed the duo to Arista Records through his recently established Star Trak imprint.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: Clipse began working on their major label debut, executively produced by The Neptunes.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: Their debut single, Grindin' was released on May 14, 2002, and became a summer Top 40 hit, reaching number 30 on the Billboard Hot 100 on July 30, 2002.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: Similar success followed with their second single, When the Last Time, which peaked at No. 19.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: Fueled by two successful singles, Clipse released their commercial debut album Lord Willin' on August 20, 2002, debuting at No. 1 on Billboard's Top R&B/Hip-hop Album chart and No. 4 on the Billboard 200, eventually being certified gold by the Recording Industry Association of America (RIAA) on October 1, 2002.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: In late 2003, Clipse began recording material for their second album, Hell Hath No Fury.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: However, further work on the album ground to a halt in 2004, when Arista Records's urban artists were absorbed into its sister label Jive Records as part of a larger merger between Sony Music Entertainment and BMG.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: Due to contractual requirements, Clipse was forced to stay on Jive, while Star Trak and the rest of its roster moved to their new home at Interscope Records.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: While Clipse resumed work on the album, and eventually finished recording it, the duo became increasingly frustrated with Jive, as the label was notorious for overlooking various hip-hop/R&B artists in favor of more pop-oriented acts on its roster.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: The label's musical strategy expansion caused numerous delays in the release of Hell Hath No Fury.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: As delays continued, the group asked for a formal release from its contract.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: When Jive refused to grant this request, the duo sued the label.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: In response to this, in 2004, the brothers launched their own record label imprint, Re-Up Records, and formed the hip hop group Re-Up Gang, along with fellow rappers Ab-Liva and Sandman.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: On May 9, 2006, Clipse finally reached an agreement with Jive to release the album through both Re-Up and Jive.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: Hell Hath No Fury was finally released on November 28, 2006.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: Once again produced by The Neptunes, it debuted at No. 14 on the Billboard 200 with over 80,000 copies sold in the 1st week.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: While the album received a great deal of critical acclaim, its sales were less successful than Lord Willin'.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: It spawned two moderately successful singles: "Mr. Me Too" with Pharrell Williams and "Wamp Wamp (What It Do)" with Slim Thug.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: Clipse's frustrations with Jive were a constant theme of the album, with Pusha T saying "I'm sorry to the fans, but them crackers weren't playing fair at Jive" on the track Mr. Me Too.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: The hip hop magazine XXL gave the album a "XXL" rating, marking it as a five-star album.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: At the time only five albums had previously received that honor.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: In a May 19, 2007, interview with Eye Weekly, Clipse revealed that they had been officially released from any contractual obligations with Jive.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: After this, the duo began discussions with several record labels, eventually signing with Columbia Records on October 26, 2007.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: The follow-up to Hell Hath No Fury, titled Til the Casket Drops, was released on December 8, 2009, via Columbia Records.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: In a departure from the group's previous works, which only featured production from the Neptunes, the album features production from Sean "Diddy" Combs' production team The Hitmen, and DJ Khalil among others.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: The album peaked at No. 41 on the Billboard 200.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: After releasing their third album, Pusha T and Malice announced Clipse would be going on indefinite hiatus so the brothers could focus on their solo careers.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: Shortly after this, Pusha T was signed to Kanye West's GOOD Music label in September 2010, and made his first appearance as a member of the GOOD roster on Kanye West's My Beautiful Dark Twisted Fantasy, appearing on his hit "Runaway" and premiering the song with him at the 2010 MTV Video Music Awards on September 12, 2010.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: He was also featured on several tracks from West's GOOD Fridays series and made other appearances on Swizz Beatz's Monster Mondays series, Lloyd Banks' H.F.M. 2 (Hunger for More 2) and Tabi Bonney's Fresh, respectively.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: On the week of December 16, 2010, Pusha T signed an exclusive management deal with NUE Agency.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: On February 11, 2011, Funkmaster Flex debuted Pusha T's debut solo single on New York City's Hot 97.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: The track, titled "My God", was produced by Hit-Boy and was generally well received by the public.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: Soon after, the song leaked onto the internet, however was not officially released through iTunes and Amazon until August 24, 2011.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: On August 31, 2011, it was announced Pusha had signed a solo record deal with Def Jam.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: On March 21, 2011, Pusha T released his solo debut, a mixtape titled Fear of God, which included "My God" and featured both freestyles and original songs, and included features from Kanye West, 50 Cent, Rick Ross, Pharrell Williams and Kevin Cossom.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: The mixtape was well received, and soon after he began working on his debut extended play (EP) Fear of God II: Let Us Pray, which initially included four songs from the mixtape and five new songs.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: The EP was originally set to be released on June 21, 2011; however, it was pushed back to August 23, and for a while September 27 was believed to be the date, but after it came and went, on October 6, 2011, Pusha T announced the EP was set to be released on November 8, 2011.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: In addition, it was revealed he had added four more songs to the EP, bringing it to 12 tracks in total.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: Considered a re-release of the initial Fear of God, it was released on November 8, 2011, and was well received by critics.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: The first single from Fear of God II: Let Us Pray was leaked onto the Internet on July 8, 2011.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: The song, titled "Trouble on My Mind", features Odd Future frontman Tyler, The Creator.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: The EP's second single, "Amen", was released September 13, 2011.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: The song, originally meant for Young Jeezy, was produced by Shawty Redd and features verses from Kanye West and Young Jeezy, respectively.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: After the EP's release on November 8, the project debuted at number 66 on the Billboard 200 with 8,900 copies sold in its first week released.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: It also entered at number ten on Billboard's R&B/Hip-Hop Albums, at number eight on Billboard's Top Rap Albums, and at number 25 on its Digital Albums chart.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: In 2011, Pusha T appeared on the second season of the HBO series How to Make It in America.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: He played the role of a henchman for Urban Caribbean League.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: After the release of his EP, Pusha T started working on his solo debut studio album, which would be executively produced by Kanye West.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: Pusha also said that after the release of his solo debut album and the Re-Up Gang mixtape, Long Live the Cane, Clipse would also reunite and release another album.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: In late 2011, Pusha made a guest appearance on English pop singer Pixie Lott's "What Do You Take Me For?", the second single from her second studio album Young Foolish Happy.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: The song was a hit single in the UK, peaking at number ten on the UK Top 40.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: Clipse then went on a full hiatus as his brother renamed himself "No Malice" and pursued a brief Christian hip-hop career.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: On October 19, 2011, via Twitter, Kanye West announced plans for a Spring 2012 GOOD Music album, featuring all artists from the label as well as numerous guest appearances.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: On April 6, 2012, "Mercy", the lead single from the GOOD Music compilation album Cruel Summer was released.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: The song, produced by newly signed in-house producer Lifted, features Pusha T along with Kanye West, Big Sean and southern rapper 2 Chainz.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: On May 24, 2012, Pusha T released a song titled "Exodus 23:1" featuring The-Dream.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: It is speculated that the song is a diss track aimed at Young Money rappers Drake and Lil Wayne.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: This resulted in a diss-song by Lil Wayne, which Pusha T did not directly respond to, but branded it as "horrible" in an interview.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: He was featured alongside West on the third single for Cruel Summer - "New God Flow".
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: In October 2012, Pusha T made an appearance on the soundtrack to the film The Man with the Iron Fists on a track titled "Tick Tock" alongside fellow American rappers Raekwon, Joell Ortiz and Danny Brown.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: On October 8, 2012, Pusha T released "Pain" featuring southern rapper Future, the first single from his debut album.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: That same day Spin magazine reported that Pusha T's debut album had been pushed back until 2013.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: While performing in Vancouver, Canada, it was reported that Pusha T announced he would be releasing a mixtape entitled Wrath of Caine preceding the release of his debut studio album.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: Later in November, Thornton announced the title of his debut studio album to be My Name Is My Name.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: On December 5, 2012, Pusha T released "Blocka" the first single from his Wrath of Caine mixtape.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: The song features Travis Scott and Popcaan.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: The music video for the song was released on December 11, 2012.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: The mixtape was released on January 28, 2013, along with the announcement of his album coming at the end of the first quarter of 2013.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: In January 2013 it was announced that Pusha would be performing at the 2013 Coachella Valley Music and Arts Festival.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: My Name Is My Name was scheduled to be released on July 16, 2013, but was pushed back to October.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: Pusha T's debut studio album was released on October 8, 2013, featuring guest appearances from Rick Ross, Young Jeezy, 2 Chainz, Big Sean, Future, Pharrell Williams, Chris Brown and Kendrick Lamar, among others.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: The album was met with acclaim from music critics and was positioned high on many "Best Albums of 2013" lists by major publications.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: The album also fared well commercially, debuting at number 4 on the US Billboard 200, selling 74,000 copies in its first week of release.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: As of July 8, 2017, the album has sold 182,000 copies in the United States.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: The album was promoted by five singles: "Pain" featuring Future, "Numbers on the Boards", "Sweet Serenade" featuring Chris Brown, "Let Me Love You" featuring Kelly Rowland, and "Nosetalgia" featuring Kendrick Lamar, along with the promotional single "Who I Am" featuring 2 Chainz and Big Sean.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: The album includes production from Kanye West, The Neptunes, The-Dream, Just Blaze, No I.D., Nottz, Don Cannon and Swizz Beatz, among others.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: In an April 2013 interview with AskMen, Pusha revealed that shortly after his debut album was released, he would finish working on his second album, titled King Push.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: In 2013, Pusha T provided guest vocals over a Vice remix of "I'll Be Gone" for the remix album, Recharged, by American rock band Linkin Park.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: On November 19, 2014, Pusha released a standalone single titled "Lunch Money," produced by Kanye West.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: In December 2014, Pusha T King Push for a Spring 2015 release.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: In May 2015, he announced the album would be pushed back to June.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: On November 9, 2015, Pusha T revealed to Billboard that he had been appointed the new president of GOOD Music.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: On November 12, 2015, Pusha T released a single titled "Untouchable", produced by Timbaland.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: On November 23, 2015, it was announced that Pusha T would release a new album, King Push – Darkest Before Dawn: The Prelude before the aforementioned King Push album, serving as a prelude to King Push.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: It was released on December 18, 2015, and received favorable reception from critics, and reached at number 20 on the Billboard 200.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: The album was executive produced by one of Pusha T's inspirations, Puff Daddy as well as manager Steven Victor.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: Darkest Before Dawn reached over 17 million streams in its first week.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: On May 31, 2016, Pusha T released the lead single from his upcoming King Push album, "Drug Dealers Anonymous" featuring Jay-Z, initially exclusively through Jay-Z's streaming service Tidal.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: In 2017, he collaborated once again with Linkin Park on the song "Good Goodbye" of the band's seventh studio album One More Light.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: In the same year, Pusha T collaborated with the virtual band Gorillaz on the song "Let Me Out" from their studio album Humanz.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: On April 19, 2018, Kanye West announced on his Twitter page that Pusha T's King Push album would be released on May 25, 2018.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: On May 23, 2018, Pusha T announced on his Twitter page that he changed the album title from King Push to Daytona.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: The album garnered controversy when West spent $85,000 to acquire the cover art: a photo of Whitney Houston's drug-filled bathroom, taken in her Atlanta, Georgia residence in 2006.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: Not only did the content of the album cover cause outside controversy, but Pusha T claims to not have agreed with the price West paid for the photo.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: On May 25, 2018, Daytona released to critical acclaim.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: It received an 86 on Metacritic, indicating "universal acclaim".
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: Subsequently, he was named the "Best Rapper Alive" by Complex for 2018 for his work on Daytona and his diss track "The Story of Adidon".
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: The album received praise from hip-hop veterans Nas and P. Diddy, calling it "a classic album" and "a modern day masterpiece".
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: In 2024, Billboard named it as the 2nd 'Most Scathing Hip-Hop Diss of All Time'.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: In February 2020, Pusha T started a new record label, Heir Wave Media Group, to sign and develop artists from the Virginia area.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: He remained the president of GOOD Music while focusing on building a roster of artists from his home state.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: In creating the label, Pusha cited his desire to recruit "album artists" who craft narratives and larger stories throughout their projects.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: Local artists were encouraged to submit music to the Heir Wave Music YouTube channel and a weekly radio show on a local station, 103 Jamz FM.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: In the label's first year, Heir Wave Music signed Kahri 1k, Shaolinn, Leeto, and WhyNotDuce.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: On February 7, 2022, Pusha T released "Diet Coke", the lead single from his fourth studio album It's Almost Dry, which was produced by Kanye West and 88-Keys.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: The music video for the single was released the next day, directed by Omar Jones, and features Pusha T and West moving around over a white backdrop, which pays direct homage to Craig Mack's Flava in Ya Ear (Remix) music video.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: 88-Keys later revealed that the beat for the single was made 18 years before the song was made, on a beat tape named The Makings of Crack Cocaine.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: On March 4, Pusha T and Nigo released the single "Hear Me Clearly" for Nigo's album I Know Nigo!, the song is also set to appear on It's Almost Dry.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: He also appeared alongside his brother (once again credited as Malice) on the Clipse song "Punch Bowl" on the I Know Nigo! album as well.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: The music video also for "Hear Me Clearly" released on March 30.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: On April 6, Pusha T released the third single for It's Almost Dry, "Neck & Wrist" featuring rapper Jay-Z and Pharrell, and would later appear in an interview with Charlamagne tha God, which released on the 11th.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: On the 18th, Pusha T announced the release date of It's Almost Dry as April 22, and also announced a listening party in New York City named "Cokechella".
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: The much-delayed album, primarily produced by frequent collaborators Pharrell Williams and Kanye West, was released on April 22 to widespread critical acclaim.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: On the week dated May 7, 2022, it debuted atop the Billboard 200 with a total of 55,000 album equivalent units, becoming Pusha T's first number-one album on the chart.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: In December 2022, Pusha T announced his departure from GOOD Music after founder Kanye West's antisemitic and pro-race remarks.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: Speaking on West's support for "White Lives Matter", his 2024 presidential campaign and other public outbursts, Pusha T stated that they were nothing to "tap dance around".
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: His departure also ended his tenure as the label's president.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: Shortly after, he changed his focus on his own label, Heir Wave Music Group.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: During an interview with Complex, Pusha T stated: "I have a particular need to build out Heir Wave as a platform and build out a circuit for artists within this region, simply because I feel like it's something that we've never had."
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: He further added: "[the label] was made in the spirit of an “album artist”—artists who have a story to tell. They have a background for the fan who wants to be fully invested in that particular artist, their whole movement, and everything about them. That's how we’re picking artists. It's about authenticity. It's about pure music, whatever type of music it is. It must be pure."
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: To promote the film, Cocaine Bear, which was released on February 24, 2023, Pusha T remade the Grandmaster Flash and Melle Mel 1983 classic, "White Lines (Don't Don't Do It)", keeping the original chorus, but replacing the original verses with his own.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: He later performed at the 22nd Coachella Valley Music and Arts Festival in April 2023.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: In November 13, 2024, Thornton announced Grindin Coffee, which takes its name from the 2002 Clipse hit "Grindin'", which will launch nationwide in 2025.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: Ahead of Clipse's reunion and fourth studio album after fifteen years, Let God Sort Em Out, Pusha T and his brother No Malice premiered an interview with GQ, where the duo revealed that they were dropped from the Def Jam label as well as Pusha T as a solo artist, and also confirmed Kendrick Lamar's appearance in their upcoming album.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: The next day, Pusha T's longtime manager Steven Victor revealed during an interview with Billboard that the rapper actually had to pay an undisclosed seven-figure sum to be dropped from the Def Jam label, in order to be released from both Clipse's and his own contractual obligations, elaborating further how the label has been suppressing Pusha T's collaborations with other artists and even his own music releases since his feud with Canadian rapper Drake in 2018.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: After Pusha T released "My God", the first single from his solo mixtape, his former GOOD Music label-mate Consequence took to Twitter and claimed Pusha T stole his flow and lyrics from a song of his that Pusha T was supposed to appear on, titled "The Last Supper".
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: On July 22, 2011, Consequence released a song titled "The Plagiarist Society" where he takes shots and questions Pusha T's coke-dealing raps.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: Towards the end of the record, the Queens native promises to take aim at Kanye West next saying "You're nothing but a body shield, for that coward from the mid-west/ so yes you can bet, that your boss is next".
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: Pusha T responded to the diss track when he appeared on Chicago's 107.5 WGCI's The Morning Riot and said nobody is looking for Consequence, as for if he would respond on a record, Pusha T went on to say "At the end of the day I am an artist and this whole rap thing is fun to me, so I can't say you won't hear nothing, but to go back and forth with him, it's not right, I won't get anything out of it."
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: Later that day, Consequence called into Chicago's WGCI's The Morning Riot in retaliation to the remarks Pusha T made about him.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: He also premiered a song titled "Everybody Told Me 2 (Straighten It Out)" where he disses West, Pusha T and GOOD Music in general.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: Since then Pusha T has responded to Consequence on a record.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: The song was the remix to Ace Hood's "Go 'N' Get It" which also featured Beanie Sigel, Busta Rhymes and Styles P. In the song Pusha raps "Consequence, nigga, talk is cheap You don't want a problem? Off the beef Before I off his ass with his awful teeth".
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: On August 19, Consequence released Movies on Demand 3 and continued to diss his former label and Pusha T on songs such as "Career Killer" and "Mr.RapFix (Hot Water)".
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: On September 15, 2011, Consequence appeared on MTV's Rap Fix and announced his feud with Kanye West and GOOD Music was over.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: While out in Chicago in October 2011, Pusha T appeared on WGCI radio for a second time, and confirmed that the "beef" was indeed over, that it had died out and they have moved on.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: In January 2015, the two officially ended the feud when Consequence took to his Instagram page to let the people know: "All G.O.O.D. in 2015, Pusha [T] and I deaded everything and we creatively vibed with Kanye for this new LP."
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: The tension between Pusha T and rapper Lil Wayne had been going on for years, beginning soon after Clipse and Birdman worked on "What Happened to That Boy", the latter's 2002 single.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: In 2006, Wayne felt the Clipse song "Mr. Me Too" was directed at him, and in 2012 Pusha T's "Exodus 23:1" song caused Lil Wayne to vent on Twitter, later releasing a diss track titled "Goulish", in which he says "Fuck Pusha T and anybody that love him / His head up his ass, I'mma have to head-butt him".
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: Pusha T has called Wayne's diss track "horrible" and said he felt it did not deserve a response.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: Both men have downplayed the feud, with Wayne saying he is over it.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: However, in September 2012, Pusha T appeared on the remix of Chief Keef's I Don't Like, where he accused Wayne of using ghostwriters saying, "My pen's better, you don't write, trendsetter, you clone-like", he has since confirmed that the line was a Wayne diss.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: In late November 2012, Pusha T once again dissed Wayne and Birdman on a Ludacris song titled "Mad Fo" from his #IDGAF mixtape.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: Pusha T later revealed his motivation for the verse: "Oh because it's a Swizz beat. You got to blame Swizz. See, when Wayne got a Swizz beat... with the "Ghoulish" track; he got busy, well he tried to."
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: After the release of Pusha T's song "Exodus 23:1" in 2012, Drake seemingly responded to Pusha on the intro to his 2013 album Nothing Was the Same, calling Pusha T a "bench player acting like a starter".
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: The two directed subliminal disses towards each other between 2012 and 2017 with Pusha T rapping on the song "H.G.T.V", "It's too far gone when the realest ain't real / I walk amongst the clouds, so your ceilings ain't real/ These niggas Call of Duty 'cause they killings ain't real / With a questionable pen so the feeling ain't real," with Drake later responding on the diss track "Two Birds, One Stone" questioning Pusha T's drug dealing past. Pusha T further escalated the feud on the song "Infrared" from his 2018 album Daytona, where he accused Drake of using a ghostwriter. Drake responded to the song less than one day later, releasing a track titled "Duppy Freestyle" where he insults both Pusha T and Kanye West, accusing Pusha of being a fake drug dealer and claiming that he would boost sales of Pusha T's album just by dissing him. Pusha T responded to Duppy on May 29, 2018, with the track "The Story of Adidon" which featured Pusha responding to Drake over the instrumental of Jay-Z's 2017 single "The Story of O.J."
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: The song debuted on Hot 97 and has lines directed towards rumors Drake has an illegitimate child and his producer's multiple sclerosis. The song additionally referenced Pusha's ongoing beef with Lil Wayne and Birdman. The song's cover art also attracted controversy, showing an unedited picture of Drake wearing a Jim Crow t-shirt and hoodie and blackface makeup. Drake eventually admitted to losing the feud in an interview with RapRadar, saying it was his "first loss in the competitive sport of rapping."
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: In a June 2016 interview, former record executive Steve Stoute claimed that Pusha T had allegedly written the McDonald's "I'm lovin' it" jingle.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: Thornton later confirmed the news on Twitter.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: However, this claim has been disputed by advertising executives who created the campaign, and a McDonald's marketing executive.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: Neither Stoute nor Pusha T have commented on the dispute.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: On March 21, 2022, Pusha T recorded a freestyle for a commercial presented by fast food chain Arby's, naming it "Spicy Fish Diss", aimed at rival fast food chain McDonald's.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: On the track, he states that their Filet-O-Fish sandwich was "disgusting", and states that Arby's Fish Sandwich is better.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: This was revenge toward the company for not crediting him for helping popularize the "I'm lovin' it" advertising campaign.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: Pusha T entered into a dispute with Jim Jones, which began in May 2023 after the latter dismissed the former on the Breakfast Club, when he claimed that he "couldn't name any top five Pusha T songs".
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: A month later, on June 25, a snippet of an unnamed diss track by Pusha T was released.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: The following week, on July 6, Jim Jones responded with "Summer Collection".
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: Podcaster Joe Budden also defended "Summer Collection", while calling Pusha T a "sore loser".
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: Jones' former collaborator and friend, Cam'ron, also sided with him in the midst of the falling out.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: Pusha's diss track titled "Chains & Whips" eventually released on July 10 exclusively on Apple Music, ahead of its release as a part of the Clipse album Let God Sort Em Out.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: On July 21, 2018, Pusha T and Virginia Williams, his girlfriend of eleven years, got married in their hometown of Virginia Beach.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: The wedding was officiated by Pusha T's brother No Malice and attended by several celebrities and Pusha T's collaborators, including Kim Kardashian, Kanye West, and best man Pharrell.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: On June 11, 2020, he and Williams welcomed their first child, Nigel Brixx Thornton.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: The child's middle name, "Brixx", attracted reactions online for being an apparent slang term for cocaine, something which Pusha T raps about often.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: On November 15, 2025, Pusha T and Williams announced they are expecting a second son together.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: In January 2026, he was found to be mentioned in the release of the Epstein files along with fellow rapper Jay-Z and sex offender Harvey Weinstein with a tip given to the FBI by an unknown person.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: In November 2021, Pusha T's mother died, as did his father four months later.
data.title: Pusha_T

data.text: Cristina Stuart Green, Lady Green (née Paine, formerly Palos; born August 1949), known as Tina Green, is an English businesswoman and interior designer.
data.title: Tina_Green

data.text: Green is the director of Taveta, the majority owner of Taveta Investments Ltd, the parent company of the Arcadia Group, of which her husband, Sir Philip Green, is chairman.
data.title: Tina_Green

data.text: The Arcadia Group owned the clothing retail chains Topshop and Topman, as well as Burton, Dorothy Perkins, Evans, Miss Selfridge, Outfit, and Wallis.
data.title: Tina_Green

data.text: Taveta owned British Homes Stores (BHS) before its 2015 sale.
data.title: Tina_Green

data.text: BHS was placed into administration in 2016, and the Arcadia Group was placed into administration in 2020.
data.title: Tina_Green

data.text: Green formed the interior design company Green & Mingarelli with the Italian designer Pietro Mingarelli.
data.title: Tina_Green

data.text: Green was the recipient of a £1.2 billion dividend payment from the Arcadia Group in 2005, a record payment in British corporate history.
data.title: Tina_Green

data.text: In 2005 The Times stated that she was "for tax reasons the legal owner" of her and her husband's estimated wealth of £4.9 billion.
data.title: Tina_Green

data.text: In 2020, the couple's wealth was estimated at £930 million by the Sunday Times Rich List and at $2.4 billion by The World's Billionaires list published by Forbes in 2021.
data.title: Tina_Green

data.text: Green has a close financial relationship with the businessman Richard Caring.
data.title: Tina_Green

data.text: She is a resident of Monaco.
data.title: Tina_Green

data.text: Cristina Stuart Paine was born in London in August 1949.
data.title: Tina_Green

data.text: Her father was a wine merchant; his business led to long periods living abroad and Green spent her childhood in Hong Kong, Japan and Thailand.
data.title: Tina_Green

data.text: Green did not finish school and described herself as "trained in nothing" but has said that she loves to "work and to graft".
data.title: Tina_Green

data.text: Green met Robert "Bobby" Palos, a South African jazz drummer in Hong Kong when she was 17 and he was 31.
data.title: Tina_Green

data.text: They married a year later in 1967 after travelling around Australia and Japan.
data.title: Tina_Green

data.text: Green initially worked in the diamond industry and subsequently moved to South Africa with Palos and the couple opened a fashion boutique in Johannesburg.
data.title: Tina_Green

data.text: Green and Palos had two children, Stasha (born 1972) and Brett (born 1974).
data.title: Tina_Green

data.text: Green's daughter, Stasha, subsequently described her mother's early career as having involved being "a diamond dealer, the first female DJ in Johannesburg [and] a go-go dancer" as well as dancing with The Beach Boys.
data.title: Tina_Green

data.text: Green and Palos later took their fashion boutique to London.
data.title: Tina_Green

data.text: Green described herself as more driven to succeed in business than Palos, and after 20 years together the couple divorced.
data.title: Tina_Green

data.text: They remained friends after their divorce and Green and Palos's second wife were at his bedside when he died.
data.title: Tina_Green

data.text: She met businessman Philip Green in 1985 and described him as "Just an ordinary person with a seriously strong work ethic", who was "a colourful character" with "zero money".
data.title: Tina_Green

data.text: They married in 1990.
data.title: Tina_Green

data.text: The couple have two children, Chloe (born 1991) and Brandon (born 1993).
data.title: Tina_Green

data.text: Green designed clothing for her husband's clothing shops, including Lewis's and Owen Owen, and subsequently helped design the layout of the stores.
data.title: Tina_Green

data.text: Green's fashion boutique in London's Knightsbridge district, Harabels, closed in 1992.
data.title: Tina_Green

data.text: Green, her husband Philip, and their children moved to Monaco in 1998, having previously lived on Avenue Road in London's St John's Wood district.
data.title: Tina_Green

data.text: Philip Green has said that the move was for health reasons.
data.title: Tina_Green

data.text: Tina Green said in a 2005 interview that the couple moved from St John's Wood to Monaco after Philip was the victim of a mugging by three men with a sword.
data.title: Tina_Green

data.text: Green has organised several large parties for her husband Philip's 50th, 55th and 60th birthday parties.
data.title: Tina_Green

data.text: Philip's 50th birthday party took place in Cyprus and cost an estimated £5 million.
data.title: Tina_Green

data.text: The party featured performances from Earth, Wind & Fire, and the singers Tom Jones and Rod Stewart.
data.title: Tina_Green

data.text: His 55th birthday party was held in the Maldives at a cost of £20 million, with performances from Jennifer Lopez and George Michael.
data.title: Tina_Green

data.text: His 60th was held at the Rosewood Mayakoba resort in Mexico featuring performances from The Beach Boys, Robbie Williams and Stevie Wonder.
data.title: Tina_Green

data.text: In 2012 Green ordered the superyacht Lionheart from the shipbuilders Benetti at an estimated cost of £100 million.
data.title: Tina_Green

data.text: Green was appointed treasurer to the private charitable foundation of Charlene, Princess of Monaco, in 2017.
data.title: Tina_Green

data.text: In 2000, she bought £25 million of shares in the British retail company Marks & Spencer shortly before it was announced that Philip Green was considering a takeover of the company.
data.title: Tina_Green

data.text: Green was described as the "for tax reasons the legal owner" of her and her husband's estimated wealth of £4.9 billion by The Times in 2005.
data.title: Tina_Green

data.text: In 2020, the couple's wealth was estimated at £930 million by the Sunday Times Rich List and at $2.4 billion by The World's Billionaires list published by Forbes in 2021.
data.title: Tina_Green

data.text: Philip and Tina Green's net worth at its peak in 2007 was estimated to be £4.9 billion by the Sunday Times Rich List, it had declined to an estimated £930 million by 2020.
data.title: Tina_Green

data.text: Green has spoken of the British public's perceived resentment of her wealth saying in a 2005 interview that she thought that " ... unfortunately, in this country [the United Kingdom] there's a lot of jealousy. No one likes a winner, they just want the bad news. I just find it very sad".
data.title: Tina_Green

data.text: In a 2012 interview Green said that it had been " ... really scary. It scares me. Yes. Because it's been so ... difficult".
data.title: Tina_Green

data.text: Green is the director of Taveta Ltd which is the majority owner of Taveta Investments Ltd.
data.title: Tina_Green

data.text: Taveta Investments Ltd is the parent company of the Arcadia Group, of which Green's husband, Philip, is the chairman.
data.title: Tina_Green

data.text: Taveta Investments acquired the Arcadia Group for £770 million in 2004, by 2018 the group owned the clothing store chains of Topshop and Topman as well as Burton, Dorothy Perkins, Evans, Miss Selfridge, Outfit, and Wallis.
data.title: Tina_Green

data.text: In 2005 Tina Green was the recipient of a £1.2 billion dividend from Arcadia, the largest dividend in British corporate history.
data.title: Tina_Green

data.text: Green notably paid no British income tax on the dividend due to her residency in the tax haven of Monaco.
data.title: Tina_Green

data.text: The dividend was paid for by a loan taken out by Arcadia, cutting Arcadia's corporation tax as interest charges on the loan were offset against profits.
data.title: Tina_Green

data.text: In August 2010 Philip Green said that "My wife's not a tax exile – my family do not live in the United Kingdom, it's somewhat different. We do pay all our tax in Britain. I think we have paid over the last five years some £300-400m in taxes on profits that have been made on our company".
data.title: Tina_Green

data.text: Philip Green has jocularly referred to his wife's income as "housekeeping money".
data.title: Tina_Green

data.text: In 2016 Green said that she or her family had controlling stakes in 11 companies, the majority of which were based in Jersey and the British Virgin Islands.
data.title: Tina_Green

data.text: Green said that the locations were chosen as they had strong regulatory and professional corporate regimes.
data.title: Tina_Green

data.text: The British Home Stores (BHS) group was acquired by Taveta for £200 million in 2000.
data.title: Tina_Green

data.text: It was subsequently sold in 2015 for £1, and went into administration in 2016.
data.title: Tina_Green

data.text: BHS had a deficit in its pension schemes of £571 million at the time of its 2016 collapse and 11,000 jobs were put at risk.
data.title: Tina_Green

data.text: The shareholders of BHS including the Green family were the recipients of £580 million from the group during their tenure.
data.title: Tina_Green

data.text: In 2016, Philip Green agreed to appear before a work and pensions select committee of the British House of Commons on condition that his wife was not called before the committee.
data.title: Tina_Green

data.text: As the largest shareholder of the Arcadia Group, in 2019 Green put £100 million over three years into the group's two pension schemes in a deal arranged with the Pensions Regulator.
data.title: Tina_Green

data.text: In 2019 Tina Green put £50 million into the Arcadia Group in exchange for rent reductions on clothing stores rented by the group from landlords.
data.title: Tina_Green

data.text: The Arcadia Group went into administration in November 2020.
data.title: Tina_Green

data.text: The group had struggled with several years of declining sales and the economic fallout of the COVID-19 pandemic in the United Kingdom.
data.title: Tina_Green

data.text: It was seen as having suffered from underinvestment in comparison to other retail companies and having failed to make as successful transition to online retail as its corporate rivals.
data.title: Tina_Green

data.text: In 2010 the Greens became the subject of protests from the activist group UK Uncut for their alleged avoidance of corporate taxation.
data.title: Tina_Green

data.text: At the time of the protests the Conservative government under Prime Minister David Cameron was imposing austerity through cuts to government expenditure.
data.title: Tina_Green

data.text: The protestors claimed that the cuts could be avoided if corporate tax avoidance was eradicated.
data.title: Tina_Green

data.text: Philip Green had been appointed by Cameron as an advisor to the government on efficiency.
data.title: Tina_Green

data.text: The UK Uncut campaigners staged a sit-in at Arcadia's flagship London Topshop store in Oxford Street and glued themselves to the windows of Topshop in Brighton on 4 December 2010.
data.title: Tina_Green

data.text: The protestors also targeted Barclays, Boots, HSBC, and Vodafone stores.
data.title: Tina_Green

data.text: Green formed the interior design company Green & Mingarelli with the Italian furniture designer Pietro Mingarelli, having met him on a yacht.
data.title: Tina_Green

data.text: The pair work up to 15 hour days when working on designs.
data.title: Tina_Green

data.text: The company has created interiors for private residences and yachts.
data.title: Tina_Green

data.text: Green's interior design work is noted for her extensive use of black and white.
data.title: Tina_Green

data.text: The company restored and designed the interior of a mews house in London's Belgravia district "almost entirely" in black and white.
data.title: Tina_Green

data.text: Green extensively uses Lalique glass in her interior designs and helped create a homewear range for Lalique Maison in 2014.
data.title: Tina_Green

data.text: Mark Harrison, writing in The Times, described Green's Lalique range as "rather lovely; ornate, but not vulgar; terribly grand" and a "harmonious, genteel, upmarket non-riot of off-white, ebony, crystal and gold".
data.title: Tina_Green

data.text: Green herself described her Lalique work as "obviously high end, and obviously expensive".
data.title: Tina_Green

data.text: Green & Mingarelli came to the attention of the owner of Lalique, Silvio Denz, due to their extensive use of Lalique glass in the decoration of the 68.5m motor yacht Silver Angel, which led to their homeware commission.
data.title: Tina_Green

data.text: In their Lalique collection a sideboard was priced at €30,000 and a mirror at €10,000.
data.title: Tina_Green

data.text: Green has been linked financially to the British businessman Richard Caring, a close friend and business partner of her husband Philip Green.
data.title: Tina_Green

data.text: It was revealed in the Swiss Leaks that Green held the "vast majority of [Caring's] cash assets" on trust for him in her bank account with HSBC in Monaco.
data.title: Tina_Green

data.text: Green provided £23.5 million to Caring to help him purchase the restaurant chains Belgo and Strada from Luke Johnson.
data.title: Tina_Green

data.text: Green gifted the Silver Angel motor yacht, worth an estimated £25 million to Caring in 2017.
data.title: Tina_Green

data.text: In 2009 Caring had told the Evening Standard newspaper that he had just acquired the yacht but it was revealed in the Pandora Papers leak that it had been held in Green's name from 2009 to 2017.
data.title: Tina_Green

data.text: Silver Angel was decorated by Green's company, Green & Mingarelli in tones of white, cream and black.
data.title: Tina_Green

data.text: When Philip Green first saw the interior of the yacht he is said to have remarked to his wife "Are these the only fucking colours you can do? It's the same colour as our boat".
data.title: Tina_Green

data.text: Anita Faye Hill (born July 30, 1956) is an American lawyer, educator and author.
data.title: Anita_Hill

data.text: She is a professor of social policy, law, and women's studies at Brandeis University and a faculty member of the university's Heller School for Social Policy and Management.
data.title: Anita_Hill

data.text: She became a national figure in 1991 when she accused U.S. Supreme Court nominee Clarence Thomas, her supervisor at the United States Department of Education and the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, of sexual harassment.
data.title: Anita_Hill

data.text: Anita Hill was born to a family of farmers in Lone Tree, Oklahoma, the youngest of Albert and Erma Hill's 13 children.
data.title: Anita_Hill

data.text: Her family came from Arkansas, where her maternal grandfather Henry Eliot and all of her great-grandparents had been born into slavery.
data.title: Anita_Hill

data.text: Hill was raised in the Baptist faith.
data.title: Anita_Hill

data.text: Hill graduated from Morris High School, Oklahoma, in 1973, where she was class valedictorian.
data.title: Anita_Hill

data.text: Hill received her bachelor's degree in psychology in 1977 from Oklahoma State University.
data.title: Anita_Hill

data.text: In 1980, she earned her Juris Doctor from Yale Law School in New Haven, Connecticut.
data.title: Anita_Hill

data.text: Hill was admitted to the District of Columbia Bar in 1980 and began her law career as an associate with the Washington, D.C. firm of Wald, Harkrader & Ross.
data.title: Anita_Hill

data.text: In 1981, she became an attorney-adviser to Clarence Thomas, who was then the Assistant Secretary of the U.S. Department of Education's Office for Civil Rights.
data.title: Anita_Hill

data.text: When Thomas became chairman of the U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) in 1982, Hill served as his assistant, leaving the job in 1983.
data.title: Anita_Hill

data.text: Hill then became an assistant professor at the evangelical Christian O. W. Coburn School of Law at Oral Roberts University where she taught from 1983 to 1986.
data.title: Anita_Hill

data.text: In 1986, she joined the faculty at the University of Oklahoma College of Law where she taught commercial law and contracts.
data.title: Anita_Hill

data.text: In 1989, she became the first tenured African American professor at OU.
data.title: Anita_Hill

data.text: She left the university in 1996 due to ongoing calls for her resignation that began after her 1991 testimony.
data.title: Anita_Hill

data.text: In 1998, she became a visiting scholar at Brandeis University and, in 2015, a university professor at the school.
data.title: Anita_Hill

data.text: In 1991, President George H. W. Bush nominated Clarence Thomas, a federal circuit judge, to succeed retiring Associate Supreme Court Justice Thurgood Marshall.
data.title: Anita_Hill

data.text: Senate hearings on his confirmation were initially completed with Thomas's good character being presented as a primary qualification for the high court because he had been a judge for just slightly more than one year.
data.title: Anita_Hill

data.text: There had been little organized opposition to Thomas's nomination, and his confirmation seemed assured until a report of a private interview of Hill by the FBI was leaked to the press.
data.title: Anita_Hill

data.text: The hearings were then reopened, and Hill was called to testify publicly.
data.title: Anita_Hill

data.text: Hill said on October 11, 1991, in televised hearings that Thomas had sexually harassed her while he was her supervisor at the Department of Education and the EEOC.
data.title: Anita_Hill

data.text: When questioned on why she followed Thomas to the second job after he had already allegedly harassed her, she said working in a reputable position within the civil rights field had been her ambition.
data.title: Anita_Hill

data.text: She also said in her testimony that she had no other job to go to.
data.title: Anita_Hill

data.text: The position at the EEOC was appealing enough to keep her from going back into private practice with her previous firm.
data.title: Anita_Hill

data.text: She said that she realized only later in her life that the choice had represented poor judgment on her part, but that "at that time, it appeared that the sexual overtures... had ended."
data.title: Anita_Hill

data.text: According to Hill, Thomas asked her out socially many times during her two years of employment as his assistant, and after she declined his requests, he used work situations to discuss sexual subjects and push advances.
data.title: Anita_Hill

data.text: "He spoke about... such matters as women having sex with animals and films showing group sex or rape scenes," she said, adding that on several occasions Thomas graphically described "his own sexual prowess" and the details of his anatomy.
data.title: Anita_Hill

data.text: Hill also recounted an instance in which Thomas examined a can of Coke on his desk and asked, "Who has put pubic hair on my Coke?"
data.title: Anita_Hill

data.text: Thomas said he had considered Hill a friend whom he had helped at every turn, so when accusations of harassment came from her, they were particularly hurtful and he said, "I lost the belief that if I did my best, all would work out."
data.title: Anita_Hill

data.text: Four female witnesses waited in the wings to support Hill's credibility, but they were not called, due to what the Los Angeles Times described as a private, compromise deal between Republicans and the Senate Judiciary Committee chair, Democrat Joe Biden.
data.title: Anita_Hill

data.text: Hill agreed to take a polygraph test.
data.title: Anita_Hill

data.text: While senators and other authorities observed that polygraph results cannot be relied upon and are inadmissible in courts, Hill's results did support her statements.
data.title: Anita_Hill

data.text: Thomas did not take a polygraph test.
data.title: Anita_Hill

data.text: He made a vehement and complete denial, saying that he was being subjected to a "high-tech lynching for uppity blacks" by white liberals who were seeking to block a black conservative from taking a seat on the Supreme Court.
data.title: Anita_Hill

data.text: After extensive debate, the United States Senate confirmed Thomas to the Supreme Court by a vote of 52–48, the narrowest margin since the 19th century.
data.title: Anita_Hill

data.text: Members questioned Hill's credibility after the timeline of her events came into question.
data.title: Anita_Hill

data.text: They mentioned the time delay of ten years between the alleged behavior by Thomas and Hill's accusations, and observed that Hill had followed Thomas to a second job and later had personal contacts with Thomas, including giving him a ride to an airport — behavior which they said would be inexplicable if Hill's allegations were true.
data.title: Anita_Hill

data.text: Hill countered that she had come forward because she felt an obligation to share information on the character and actions of a person who was being considered for the Supreme Court.
data.title: Anita_Hill

data.text: She testified that after leaving the EEOC, she had had two "inconsequential" phone conversations with Thomas, and had seen him personally on two occasions, once to get a job reference and the second time when he made a public appearance in Oklahoma where she was teaching.
data.title: Anita_Hill

data.text: Doubts about the veracity of Hill's 1991 testimony persisted among conservatives long after Thomas took his seat on the Court.
data.title: Anita_Hill

data.text: They were furthered by right-wing magazine American Spectator writer David Brock in his 1993 book The Real Anita Hill, though he later recanted the claims he had made which he described in his book as "character assassination," and apologized to Hill.
data.title: Anita_Hill

data.text: After interviewing a number of women who alleged that Thomas had frequently subjected them to sexually explicit remarks, The Wall Street Journal reporters Jane Mayer and Jill Abramson wrote, Strange Justice: The Selling of Clarence Thomas, a book that concluded that Thomas had lied during his confirmation process.
data.title: Anita_Hill

data.text: Richard Lacayo in his 1994 review of the book for Time magazine remarked, however, that "Their book doesn't quite nail that conclusion."
data.title: Anita_Hill

data.text: In 2007, Kevin Merida, a co-author of another book on Thomas, remarked that what happened between Thomas and Hill was "ultimately unknowable" by others, but that it was clear that "one of them lied, period."
data.title: Anita_Hill

data.text: Writing in 2007, Neil Lewis of The New York Times remarked that, "To this day, each side in the epic he-said, she-said dispute has its unmovable believers."
data.title: Anita_Hill

data.text: In 2007, Thomas published his autobiography, My Grandfather's Son, in which he revisited the controversy, calling Hill his "most traitorous adversary", and writing that pro-choice liberals, who feared he would vote to overturn Roe v. Wade if he were seated on the Supreme Court, used the scandal against him.
data.title: Anita_Hill

data.text: He described Hill as touchy and apt to overreact, and her work at the EEOC as mediocre.
data.title: Anita_Hill

data.text: He acknowledged that three other former EEOC employees had backed Hill's story, but said they had all left the agency on bad terms.
data.title: Anita_Hill

data.text: He also wrote that Hill "was a left-winger who'd never expressed any religious sentiments whatsoever ... and the only reason why she'd held a job in the Reagan administration was because I'd given it to her."
data.title: Anita_Hill

data.text: Hill denied the accusations in an op-ed in The New York Times saying she would not "stand by silently and allow [Justice Thomas], in his anger, to reinvent me."
data.title: Anita_Hill

data.text: In October 2010, Thomas's wife Virginia, a conservative activist, left a voicemail at Hill's office asking that Hill apologize for her 1991 testimony.
data.title: Anita_Hill

data.text: Hill initially believed the call was a hoax and referred the matter to the Brandeis University campus police who alerted the FBI.
data.title: Anita_Hill

data.text: After being informed that the call was indeed from Virginia Thomas, Hill told the media that she did not believe the message was meant to be conciliatory and said, "I testified truthfully about my experience and I stand by that testimony."
data.title: Anita_Hill

data.text: Virginia Thomas responded that the call had been intended as an "olive branch".
data.title: Anita_Hill

data.text: Shortly after the Thomas confirmation hearings, President George H. W. Bush dropped his opposition to a bill that gave harassment victims the right to seek federal damage awards, back pay, and reinstatement, and the law was passed by Congress.
data.title: Anita_Hill

data.text: In their anthology, All the Women Are White, All the Blacks Are Men, but Some of Us Are Brave, editors Gloria T. Hull, Patricia Bell-Scott, and Barbara Smith described black feminists mobilizing "a remarkable national response to the Anita Hill–Clarence Thomas controversy. In 1992, a feminist group began a nationwide fundraising campaign and then obtained matching state funds to endow a professorship at the University of Oklahoma College of Law in honor of Hill. Conservative Oklahoma state legislators reacted by demanding Hill's resignation from the university, then introducing a bill to prohibit the university from accepting donations from out-of-state residents, and finally attempting to pass legislation to close down the law school. Elmer Zinn Million, a local activist, compared Hill to Lee Harvey Oswald, the assassin of President Kennedy. Certain officials at the university attempted to revoke Hill's tenure. After five years of pressure, Hill resigned. The University of Oklahoma Law School defunded the Anita F. Hill professorship in May 1999, without the position having ever been filled. On April 25, 2019, the presidential campaign team for Joe Biden for the 2020 United States presidential election disclosed that he had called Hill to express "his regret for what she endured" in his role as the chairman of the Senate Judiciary Committee, presiding over the Thomas confirmation hearings. Hill said the call from Biden left her feeling "deeply unsatisfied". On June 13, 2019, Hill clarified that she did not consider Biden's actions disqualifying, and would be open to voting for him. In May 2020, Hill argued that sexual assault allegations made against Donald Trump as well as the sexual assault allegation against Biden should be investigated and their results "made available to the public.

data.text: " On September 5, 2020, it was reported that Hill had vowed to vote for Biden and to work with him on gender issues. Hill continued to teach at the University of Oklahoma, though she spent two years as a visiting professor in California. She resigned her post in October 1996 and finished her final semester of teaching there. In her final semester, she taught a law school seminar on civil rights. An endowed chair was created in her name, but was later defunded without ever having been filled. Hill accepted a position as a visiting scholar at the Institute for the Study of Social Change at University of California, Berkeley in January 1997, but soon joined the faculty of Brandeis University—first at the Women's Studies Program, later moving to the Heller School for Social Policy and Management. In 2011, she also took a counsel position with the Civil Rights & Employment Practice group of the plaintiffs' law firm Cohen Milstein. Over the years, Hill has provided commentary on gender and race issues on national television programs, including 60 Minutes, Face the Nation, and Meet the Press. She has been a speaker on the topic of commercial law as well as race and women's rights. She is also the author of articles that have been published in The New York Times and Newsweek and has contributed to many scholarly and legal publications in the areas of international commercial law, bankruptcy, and civil rights. In 1995, Hill co-edited Race, Gender and Power in America: The Legacy of the Hill-Thomas Hearings with Emma Coleman Jordan. In 1997 Hill published her autobiography, Speaking Truth to Power, in which she chronicled her role in the Clarence Thomas confirmation controversy and wrote that creating a better society had been a motivating force in her life. She contributed the piece "The Nature of the Beast: Sexual Harassment" to the 2003 anthology Sisterhood Is Forever: The Women's Anthology for a New Millennium, edited by Robin Morgan. In 2011, Hill published her second book, Reimagining Equality: Stories of Gender, Race, and Finding Home, which focuses on the sub-prime lending crisis that resulted in the foreclosure of many homes owned by African-Americans. She calls for a new understanding about the importance of a home and its place in the American Dream. On March 26, 2015, the Brandeis Board of Trustees unanimously voted to recognize Hill with a promotion to Private University Professor of Social Policy, Law, and Women's Studies. On December 16, 2017, the Commission on Sexual Harassment and Advancing Equality in the Workplace was formed, selecting Hill to lead its charge against sexual harassment in the entertainment industry. The new initiative was spearheaded by co-chair of the Nike Foundation Maria Eitel, venture capitalist Freada Kapor Klein, Lucasfilm President Kathleen Kennedy and talent attorney Nina Shaw. The report found not only a saddening prevalence of continued bias but also stark differences in how varying demographics perceived discrimination and harassment. In September 2018, Hill wrote an op-ed in The New York Times regarding sexual assault allegations made by Christine Blasey Ford during the Brett Kavanaugh Supreme Court nomination. On November 8, 2018, Anita Hill spoke at the USC Dornsife event "From Social Movement to Social Impact: Putting an End to Sexual Harassment in the Workplace.

data.text: " In 1994, Hill wrote a tribute to Thurgood Marshall, the first African American Supreme Court Justice who preceded Clarence Thomas, titled "A Tribute to Thurgood Marshall: A Man Who Broke with Tradition on Issues of Race and Gender". She outlined Marshall's contributions to the principles of equality as a judge and how his work has affected the lives of African Americans, specifically African American women. On October 20, 1998, Hill published the book Speaking Truth to Power. Throughout much of the book she gives details on her side of the sexual harassment controversy, and her professional relationship with Clarence Thomas. Aside from that, she also provides a glimpse of what her personal life was like all the way from her childhood days growing up in Oklahoma to her position as a law professor. Hill became a proponent for women's rights and feminism. This can be seen through the chapter she wrote in the 2007 book Women and leadership: the state of play and strategies for change. She wrote about women judges and why, in her opinion, they play such a large role in balancing the judicial system. She argues that since women and men have different life experiences, ways of thinking, and histories, both are needed for a balanced court system. She writes that in order for the best law system to be created in the United States, all people need the ability to be represented. In 2011, Hill's second book, Reimagining Equality: Stories of Gender, Race, and Finding Home was published. She discusses the relationship between the home and the American Dream. She also exposes the inequalities within gender and race and home ownership. She argues that inclusive democracy is more important than debates about legal rights. She uses her own history and history of other African American women such as Nannie Helen Burroughs, in order to strengthen her argument for reimagining equality altogether. On September 28, 2021, Hill published the book Believing: Our Thirty-Year Journey to End Gender Violence. Hill received the American Bar Association's Commission on Women in the Profession's "Women of Achievement" award in 1992.
